topics: 🫒 The Medium Olive — the halakhic olive-bulk is neither large nor small, and why it is called 'aguri'
🍗 Bar Kappara's Two Students — who blesses first, the cabbage or the pullet? A lesson in humility
🥬 Turnips, Beets and Their Water — how cutting, flour and cooking change (or don't change) a blessing
🌿 Dill Water — Rav Pappa's dilemma, solved from the laws of teruma
🍞 Bless, Then Break — Rabbi Ḥiyya vs. Rava on when the blessing over bread must end
🥖 Piece or Whole Loaf? — Rav Huna, Rabbi Yoḥanan, and the God-fearing solution of Mar son of Ravina
🕯️ Two Loaves on Shabbat, Broken Matza on Pesaḥ — 'twice as much bread' and 'bread of affliction'

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Vegetables, Loaves, and the Etiquette of Blessing
overview.subtitle: Berakhot 39a–39b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf opens by settling the size of the halakhic olive: a medium olive, so an olive whose pit was removed still counted. It then tells the sobering story of two students before bar Kappara who quarreled over which blessing to say first, and neither lived out the year. A cluster of amoraic rulings follows on cooked turnips, beets, dill water and the flour added to a dish. The second half turns to bread: does the blessing have to end as the loaf is broken (Rabbi Ḥiyya) or is the blessing said over a whole loaf first (Rava, whose view is the halakha)? Should one bless over a piece or a whole loaf? The daf closes with the two loaves of Shabbat, the broken matza of Pesaḥ, and Rav Ami and Rav Asi using the eiruv bread for a second mitzva.

slides.title: 🍗 Bar Kappara's Students: Whose Blessing Comes First?
slides.subtitle: Cabbage, Damascene plums and pullets were set before the teacher

steps.content: 1️⃣ Bar Kappara gave one student permission to bless. He hurried and blessed the pullet first
2️⃣ His fellow student ridiculed him for grabbing the meat before the vegetables
3️⃣ Bar Kappara: 'I am not angry at the one who blessed but at the one who ridiculed. If your friend is like one who never tasted meat, why mock him?'
4️⃣ Then he turned: 'No, I am angry at the one who blessed. אִם חׇכְמָה אֵין כָּאן, זִקְנָה אֵין כָּאן?! If there is no wisdom here, is there no elder here to ask?'
5️⃣ It was taught: both students did not live out the year

6️⃣ The Gemara's lesson: was this a dispute over the blessing itself (shehakol on both, so the favorite goes first vs. ha'adama on vegetables, so the 'fruit' goes first)? No — all agree both get shehakol; they argued whether the favorite or the nourishing cabbage takes precedence

callout.label: Why the story is cited:
callout.text: The Gemara wanted to prove that tanna'im disputed whether boiled vegetables get 'Who creates fruit of the ground'. It concludes the story proves nothing about that; the students argued only about precedence.

slides.title: 🥬 Turnips, Beets, and the Water They Were Cooked In
slides.subtitle: Rulings that Rabbi Zeira, Rav Ashi and Rav Pappa brought home from their teachers
rows: Rav Huna: Who creates fruit of the ground
Rav Yehuda: fruit of the ground
Rav Huna: shehakol — they are significantly changed
Rav Yehuda: still fruit of the ground; cutting only sweetens the flavor
Rav Kahana: fruit of the ground
Turnip dish with lots of flour
Rav Kahana: Who creates various kinds of nourishment
Rav Kahana retracted: fruit of the ground — the flour is only to make it stick together
Water of beets, turnips, any boiled vegetable
Rav Pappa: clearly has the status of the vegetable
Rav Pappa's dilemma: added for flavor, or only to absorb filth?
Mishna in Okatzin: dill that gave its taste to the pot is no longer teruma or food — so it is added to sweeten the taste

callout.label: Health aside:
callout.text: Rav Ḥisda: a cooked dish of beets is good for the heart, good for the eyes, and all the more so for the intestines. Abaye: only when it sits on the stove and boils with a 'tukh tukh' sound.

slides.title: 🍞 When Must the Blessing Over Bread End?
slides.subtitle: Dry bread in a bowl sparks a dispute about the order of blessing and breaking

lines.speaker: R' Ḥiyya b. Ashi
lines.text: Over dry bread soaking in a bowl one recites hamotzi — it is bread in every respect, even if a whole loaf is also on the table.

lines.speaker: Rabbi Ḥiyya
lines.text: I disagree. צָרִיךְ שֶׁתִּכְלֶה בְּרָכָה עִם הַפַּת — the blessing must conclude together with the breaking of the loaf. Dry crumbs were sliced off long ago.

lines.speaker: Rava
lines.text: What is different about dry bread? Because the blessing ends on a slice? When you bless over a loaf too, the blessing ends on a slice, since one cuts before the blessing!

lines.speaker: Rava
lines.text: Rather: מְבָרֵךְ וְאַחַר כָּךְ בּוֹצֵעַ — one recites the blessing over the whole loaf and only afterward breaks it.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: The Sages of Neharde'a acted like Rabbi Ḥiyya; the Rabbis acted like Rava. Ravina: 'My mother told me your father acted like Rabbi Ḥiyya.'

lines.speaker: Halakha
lines.text: The halakha is in accordance with Rava: bless first, then break.

callout.label: Practical result:
callout.text: Because the blessing is completed over an intact loaf, one should not cut into it before finishing the words of hamotzi.

slides.title: 🥖 Pieces and Whole Loaves on the Same Table
slides.subtitle: Which one receives the blessing?

boxes.title: Rav Huna
items: Bless over the pieces and exempt the whole loaves
Parallel: the first tanna in teruma — separate teruma from a whole small onion, not half a large one? No, the Gemara rejects that mapping

boxes.title: Rabbi Yoḥanan
items: שְׁלֵמָה מִצְוָה מִן הַמּוּבְחָר — the whole loaf is the optimal way
Everyone agrees: a wheat piece beats a barley whole loaf; quality wins

boxes.title: The God-fearing way
items: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: a God-fearing person satisfies both — Mar son of Ravina placed the piece inside the whole loaf and broke them together
A tanna named Shalman taught the same baraita; Rav Naḥman: 'You are peace (shalom) and your teaching is whole (shelema), for you made peace among the students'

callout.label: Why the onion parallel fails:
callout.text: Where a priest is present, everyone agrees the better half-onion is given. The tanna'im disagree only when no priest is there: separate from what will endure (first tanna) or always from the best (Rabbi Yehuda). So it is not a 'whole vs. significant' dispute at all.

slides.title: 🕯️ Shabbat Loaves, Pesaḥ Matza, and the Eiruv Bread
slides.subtitle: Special occasions change how bread is broken

nodes.content: ❓ Does the 'piece inside the whole' method ever become obligatory?

columns.label: Pesaḥ
columns.content: Rav Pappa: everyone agrees one places the broken matza inside the whole and breaks — לֶחֶם עֹנִי, 'bread of affliction' (Deut. 16:3), and the poor eat pieces

columns.label: Shabbat
columns.content: Rabbi Abba: one must break bread over two loaves — לֶחֶם מִשְׁנֶה, 'twice as much bread' (Exodus 16:22) of the manna

nodes.content: 👀 Rav Ashi saw Rav Kahana hold two loaves and break one. Rabbi Zeira broke off one piece big enough for the whole Shabbat meal
🤔 Ravina: doesn't that look gluttonous? Rav Ashi: since he does not do so on other days and only does so today, it shows honor for the mitzva, not gluttony
✅ Rav Ami and Rav Asi would say hamotzi over the eiruv bread: 'since one mitzva was done with it, let us do another mitzva with it'

callout.label: Pattern:
callout.text: Each Shabbat and festival practice is anchored in a verse: the manna's double portion, and the affliction bread of the Exodus.

summary.principle: Blessings follow the food as it actually is and the loaf as it actually is: a medium olive, a turnip that is still a turnip, and a whole loaf blessed before it is broken.

flowSteps.content: 🫒 The halakhic olive is a medium olive (aguri) — even an olive minus its pit kept the measure
🍗 Bar Kappara's students: favorite first vs. nourishing cabbage first — both received shehakol; neither lived out the year
🥬 Turnips cut small, turnips with flour, vegetable water: still 'fruit of the ground'; dill water too, since dill is added for taste

columns.content: 🍞 Rabbi Ḥiyya: blessing ends as you break. Rava: bless, then break — halakha like Rava
🥖 Piece vs. whole: Mar son of Ravina puts the piece inside the whole and breaks both

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: On Pesaḥ the broken matza (bread of affliction) and on Shabbat two loaves (twice as much bread) — verses shape how the loaf is broken

quiz.q: Why did the olive brought before Rabbi Yoḥanan still count as the required measure after its pit was removed?
o: Because the pit counts toward the measure
Because the required measure is a medium olive, and that olive had been a large one
Because Rabbi Yoḥanan holds that no minimum measure is needed for a blessing after eating
Because olives are one of the seven species
quiz.e: The Gemara explains that we require only a medium ('aguri') olive; the olive brought to Rabbi Yoḥanan was large, so even without its pit the requisite measure remained.

quiz.q: What was bar Kappara's final complaint against the student who recited the blessing over the pullet?
o: He should have recited 'Who creates fruit of the ground' over the pullet
He should have asked the elder present instead of deciding on his own
He should have let his fellow student recite the blessing
He ate the pullet before the cabbage was fully cooked
quiz.e: Bar Kappara said, 'If there is no wisdom here, is there no elder here?' — the student should have asked him which blessing to recite first.

quiz.q: According to Rav Yehuda, what blessing is recited over turnip heads cut into small pieces?
o: By whose word all things came to be
Who creates various kinds of nourishment
Who creates fruit of the ground, since the fine cutting only sweetens the flavor
Who creates fruit of the tree
quiz.e: Rav Huna distinguished between large and small pieces, but Rav Yehuda taught that both get 'Who creates fruit of the ground'; the extensive cutting is merely to sweeten the taste.

quiz.q: What is the halakha regarding the order of the blessing and the breaking of bread?
o: In accordance with Rabbi Ḥiyya: the blessing must conclude as the loaf is broken
In accordance with Rava: recite the blessing over the whole loaf and then break it
One breaks the bread first and then recites the blessing
It depends on whether the bread is dry
quiz.e: Although the Sages of Neharde'a followed Rabbi Ḥiyya, the Gemara concludes that the halakha follows Rava: bless first, then break.

quiz.q: How did Mar son of Ravina satisfy both Rav Huna and Rabbi Yoḥanan when pieces and whole loaves were before him?
o: He recited two separate blessings
He always chose the wheat bread
He placed the piece inside the whole loaf and broke them together
He ate only the whole loaf
quiz.e: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak called him God-fearing because by breaking the piece together with the whole loaf he fulfilled both opinions.
